claims.claim: Sheep and Grain (ETCSL 5.3.2, 193 lines) is a Sumerian disputation in which the sisters Grain and Sheep debate their relative merits before Enlil, ending with Enlil's verdict delivered through Enki's proposal.
claims.evidence: ETCSL 5.3.2 full translation read and verified; Alster & Vanstiphout 1987, Kramer 1963, Klein 1997, Sefati 1998 (not read in full text).

claims.claim: The manuscripts of Sheep and Grain are Old Babylonian, c. 1900–1600 BCE, predominantly from Nippur.
claims.evidence: ETCSL 5.3.2 full translation read and verified; CDLI composite Q000761 confirms the manuscript picture (Old Babylonian, Nippur). Adapted from the dossier row: the scribal-curriculum and composition-date parts are not asserted in this claim.

claims.claim: Sheep and Grain illuminates the motif-level analogy of the farmer/shepherd pairing in Gen 4 (shepherd's animal offering regarded, farmer's grain offering not regarded).
claims.evidence: The pairing is genuine at motif level; the sheep here is a goddess whose value is never questioned; Grain is declared greater, yet the sisters 'stand together.'

claims.claim: Sheep and Grain illuminates why Abel's offering was regarded in Gen 4:3–5.
claims.evidence: No offering is made in Sheep and Grain; no offering is rejected; no murder occurs; the verdict direction is reversed (Grain declared greater, the grain-sister wins). The text provides no causal explanation for Gen 4:3–5.

claims.claim: Grain, bread, beer, and fruit were central, daily, legitimate divine food in Mesopotamian offering practice, and grain was never a rejected category.
claims.evidence: Nebuchadnezzar II 011 (ORACC RIBO Q005482, reigned 604–562 BCE) — ginû provisioning; SAA 07 212 (ORACC P335834, 7th c. BCE) — daily ginû for Aššur, including grain/bread.

claims.assessment: Established (absence; the searches were systematic across the consulted sources).
claims.claim: No ANE text or artefact has been found in which a god places a mark on a person to protect them from being killed.
claims.evidence: No ANE text/artefact found where a god places a mark on a person to protect them from being killed — the headline finding of Researcher A.

claims.claim: A female mummy from Deir el-Medina bears at least 30 tattoos (wadjet-eyes, seated baboons, nefer-signs, snakes).
claims.evidence: Austin & Gobeil 2017 (BIFAO 116, 23–46) — female mummy from Deir el-Medina, at least 30 tattoos (wadjet-eyes, seated baboons, nefer-signs, snakes) on neck, shoulders, arms, back. Adapted from the dossier row: the Ramesside date and the body locations are not asserted in this claim (the prose keeps 'Ramesside mummy').

claims.claim: The Deir el-Medina mummy's tattoos were probably drawn amulets (prophylactic).
claims.evidence: Austin & Gobeil 2017 (p. 28) — 'drawn amulets' reading, probable (authors' own argued interpretation, not textual statement). Adapted from the dossier row: 'probably' added and the reading qualified as the authors' argued interpretation, not a textual statement.

claims.claim: The form of the mark of Cain is known.
claims.evidence: Form unknown; Westermann refuses to answer — the most defensible position.

claims.claim: The function of the mark of Cain was protective.
claims.evidence: K&D, Ryle, Skinner, Gunkel, Westermann, JE — protective function established.

claims.assessment: Established false — no general murder law.
claims.claim: The Code of Hammurabi contains a general law against murder.
claims.evidence: Hammurabi (King translation via Hanover, opened in full; reign c. 1792–1750 BCE, Middle Chronology; stele Louvre Sb 8, Susa Dec 1901–Jan 1902, Scheil 1902) — no general murder law.

claims.claim: In Old Babylonian Babylonia, homicide was handled by state procedure, not by a blood avenger; blood feud was a northern (Assyrian/Mari) practice.
claims.evidence: Barmash thesis — probable (southern Babylonian state procedure vs. northern blood feud; no blood avenger in OB Babylonia); second-hand via the opened Bloch article (Barmash's JNES article and book not opened).

claims.claim: Hammurabi §§206–214 (brawl, oath, silver compensation) and §210 (vicarious talion), §§229–231 (negligence), §§250–252 (goring ox), and §153 (impalement — the only clear deliberate-murder case) are established.
Middle Assyrian Laws A §10 and B §2 (12th century BCE) address homicide.
claims.evidence: MAL A §10 / B §2 — probable (12th c. BCE); second-hand via the opened Encyclopedia.com synthesis (Roth's edition not opened).

claims.claim: Hittite Laws §§1–5 (c. 1500 BCE) and the Telipinu Edict §49 (c. 1500 BCE) address homicide, normally by compensation.
claims.evidence: Hittite Laws §§1–5, Telipinu §49 (c. 1500 BCE) — probable. Adapted from the dossier row: the assessment is simplified to 'Probable.'; the 'HL §6 not-independently-verified' caveat and the established generalisation are not asserted in this claim.

claims.assessment: Established absence — no such formula found in the ANE sources consulted; probable that no such formula exists in the wider collections.
claims.claim: A sevenfold vengeance formula exists in ANE sources.
claims.evidence: No sevenfold formula found in ANE sources consulted; probable no such formula in wider collections.

claims.claim: Gen 4 reverses ANE polarity: in the ANE, the murderer is punished or compensated; in Gen 4, God protects the murderer.
claims.evidence: Gen 4 reverses ANE polarity — God protects the murderer (decisive contrast).

claims.claim: No literary dependence between Gen 4 and any ANE text has been established.
claims.evidence: No literary dependence established.

claims.claim: The text of Gen 4:3–5 gives no reason why Abel's offering was regarded and Cain's was not.
claims.evidence: Offering silence established (Westermann pp. 295–296; Ryle; JE; Gunkel p. 43 — something missing, originally an Opferschau).

claims.claim: Abel's offering was regarded because of its quality (he chose the best).
claims.evidence: Quality reading debated; Westermann rejects it; Gunkel says the saga says nothing of Abel's piety; Skinner rejects it as 'arbitrary'; K&D combine it with the heart reading; JE (Rabbinical Literature) supports it.

claims.assessment: Debated (as an explanation of the narrative itself); traditional as NT reception.
claims.claim: Abel's offering was regarded because of his faith (Heb 11:4).
claims.evidence: Faith reading debated; Heb 11:4 cited by K&D, Ryle, Clarke, Westermann; Westermann: the NT reading's presupposition 'is not derived from the text.'

claims.claim: Abel's offering was regarded because of the giver's heart or disposition.
claims.evidence: Heart reading debated; K&D and Ryle support it; Gunkel/Westermann reject it as a 'modern intrusion' / 'wird von der Sage nicht geteilt.'

claims.claim: Abel's offering was regarded because it was animal (not vegetable) — shepherd's offering vs. farmer's offering.
claims.evidence: Material reading debated; Skinner leans toward it; Gunkel supports it; Westermann rejects it ('most unlikely').

claims.assessment: Established false (as a technical grain offering); established as a general gift/present offering.
claims.claim: Minḥah (H4503) in Gen 4:3–5 is a technical grain offering.
claims.evidence: BDB minḥâ sense 3 general offering (Gen 4:3–5), not technical grain offering (senses 4–5 Priestly/exilic).

claims.claim: BDB reads Gen 4:7 ḥaṭṭāʾt (H2403) as 'sin,' not 'sin offering.'
claims.evidence: BDB H2403 — reads 4:7 as 'sin is a crouching beast,' not 'sin offering.'

claims.claim: Gen 4:7 refers to a sin offering lying at the door.
claims.evidence: Sin-offering reading debated; verified supporters Clarke, JFB, Christ Over All (citing HALOT 306, DCH 3:198–200 second-hand); no verified modern commentary adopts it; five verified commentaries do not entertain it — that is not a rejection.

claims.claim: Gen 4:7 refers to sin as a crouching beast.
claims.evidence: Sin-as-beast reading debated; K&D, Ryle, Skinner, JFB (first interpretation), Gunkel (with objections); BDB tešûqâ 'of beast to devour, figurative, Gen 4:7.'

claims.claim: Gen 4:7 refers to a doorstep demon (rābiṣu).
claims.evidence: Rābiṣu demon reading debated; proposed by Duhm et al. (second-hand via Westermann); Westermann: 'very unlikely'; Gunkel: 'erwägenswert' (worth considering).

claims.claim: The wording of Gen 4:7b is identical to Gen 3:16b.
claims.evidence: Wording identical established; all five verified commentaries note it.

claims.claim: The antecedent of Gen 4:7b ('his desire… you shall rule over him') is Abel.
claims.evidence: Antecedent debated; usually Sin personified, less commonly Abel; Clarke and Christ Over All (via Turretin, second-hand) support Abel; BDB supports sin-as-beast.

claims.claim: The text of Gen 4:6–7 is corrupt, or vv. 6–7 are a later addition.
claims.evidence: Corruption debated (Ryle/Skinner/Gunkel — text probably corrupt) vs. later addition (Westermann — vv. 6–7 a later addition whose purpose is to ascribe full responsibility to Cain).

claims.claim: 'Sevenfold' (Gen 4:15, H7659 šibʿātayim) means seven of the murderer's clan will be killed in revenge.
claims.evidence: Seven kin proposed — Skinner, Ryle, Gunkel (with Stade, second-hand, ZAW XIV 297).

claims.claim: 'Sevenfold' (Gen 4:15) is a legal ordinance or deterrent — a threat of sevenfold punishment.
claims.evidence: Legal ordinance/deterrent proposed — Westermann (with Liedke, second-hand), Cassuto (second-hand), Gevirtz VT 11 (1961) 154 (second-hand), Williams VT 14 (1964) 488 (second-hand).

claims.claim: 'Sevenfold' (Gen 4:15) means seven as completeness.
claims.evidence: Completeness traditional — Smith's (1863), ATS (1859), Easton's (1897) 'Seven' only.

claims.assessment: Established (as the scholarly reading of the verse).
claims.claim: 'Am I my brother's keeper?' (Gen 4:9) is a defiant, false, mocking reply — a renunciation of brotherhood.
claims.evidence: Keeper defiance established; K&D, Ryle, Skinner, Gunkel, Westermann — defiance, falsehood, mocking joke on Abel's occupation, renunciation of brotherhood.

claims.claim: The mark of Cain was a mark of dark skin, or a racial mark.
claims.evidence: Racist misreading — no textual basis established; LDS essay (S11): the view dates from at least the 1730s; restriction 1852–1978, Official Declaration 2; 2013 disavowal quoted in the dossier.

claims.claim: Hebrews 12:24 alludes to Abel's blood ('the blood of sprinkling that speaketh better things than that of Abel').
claims.evidence: Heb 12:24 established; Ryle's 'Hebrews 12:14' is an OCR error for 12:24.

claims.claim: Gen 4:8 (MT) contains a speech ellipsis — Cain speaks to Abel but no words are quoted.
claims.evidence: 4:8 MT speech ellipsis established (verified from the OL word rows). The LXX/Samaritan supply ('Let us go into the field') is unverified and is NOT part of this claim; it must not enter the article (dossier §9, clm-ca-097, adapted at drafting — see review.notes).

claims.claim: Tešûqâ (H8669) occurs 3 times in the Hebrew Bible: Gen 3:16, Gen 4:7, Song 7:10 — the echo is exclusive to these three verses.
claims.evidence: Tešûqâ global 3: Gen 3:16, Gen 4:7, Song 7:10 — echo exclusive.

claims.claim: The ground-curse in Gen 4:11 echoes Gen 3:17 (ʾārûr H779 at 3:17 and 4:11).
claims.evidence: Ground-curse echo (ʾārûr H779 at 3:17 and 4:11) verified.

claims.claim: Nod is H5113, a hapax legomenon (global total 1).
claims.evidence: Nod H5113 (hapax, global total 1).

claims.claim: Qānâ (H7069, 'I have gotten') in Gen 4:1 is a wordplay on Cain's name, not a certain etymology.
claims.evidence: Qānâ wordplay vs. etymology debated; Gen 4:1 etymology is the text's own explanation; BDB: the name is in fact the Kenite eponym.

claims.assessment: Unknown — who they are is unknown.
claims.claim: 'Every one that findeth me' (Gen 4:14) refers to identifiable persons.
claims.evidence: 'Every one that findeth me' (4:14) — who they are unknown.

claims.claim: 'East of Eden' (Gen 4:16) reuses the east-of-Eden motif from Gen 3:24 (clm-ae-022).
claims.evidence: East-of-Eden probable reuse (clm-ae-022).

connections.note: The primary account: the births and occupations, the offerings and God's regard, the warning, the murder, the blood crying from the ground, the curse and wandering, the mark and sevenfold protection, and the departure to Nod.

The desire and rule wording of Gen 4:7b is identical to Gen 3:16b — tešûqâ occurs only three times in the Bible (Gen 3:16, Gen 4:7, Song 7:10). What the shared wording means is debated; the echo itself is a textual observation, not an interpretation.
The ground-curse echo: ʾārûr at Gen 3:17 ('cursed is the ground') and Gen 4:11 ('cursed art thou from the ground'). The tiller is cursed from the ground he tilled, which then refuses him.
Expulsion continues eastward: the cherubim stand at the east of the garden (3:24), and Cain goes further east, to Nod (4:16). A literary motif, not geography.

The sequel in the Cain's Descendants event (Gen 4:17–24): Enoch, the first city, Jabal, Jubal, Tubal-cain, and Lamech's song, including the seventy-sevenfold echo of 4:15. One-way link; the other event's record is not edited here.

Seth's birth as the narrative's continuation after Abel, and the genealogy tracing Adam's likeness to his son. Overlaps conn-ae-005, which links the same range from Adam and Eve with a distinct reason — editor to confirm both stand.
Reception: 'by faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain.' The New Testament reading of the offering; not what Genesis 4 itself states about why Abel's offering was regarded.
Reception: 'the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.' A new find, not in the research plan; Abel's blood as the measure of a better speaking.
Reception: 'not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.' The range, not 3:12 alone; Cain set as the type of the evil deed and of hatred of one's brother.
Reception: 'the way of Cain' — Cain as the type of a path others follow; a single verse, not a narration of the event.

Reception: 'the blood of righteous Abel' — Abel admitted to the ranks of the martyrs, the first righteous blood shed. Luke 11:51 carries the same saying and is retained as a supporting parallel (conn-ca-012); Matthew is primary.

Reception, supporting parallel to the primary connection conn-ca-011 (Matthew 23:35): the same saying, naming 'the blood of Abel' among the righteous blood shed. Matthew 23:35 is the primary connection; Luke 11:51 is retained as a supporting parallel.

review.notes: Draft 2026-11-14 (merged as PR #177, main 830ecb5). Phase 2 publication-readiness follow-up 2026-11-14 (branch from main 630d718; QA PASS on PR #177, head 89e5001). Stage 1 dossier 2026-11-14 (three parallel researchers: ANE parallels; Scripture connections + Hebrew lemmas; scholarship verification + synthesis). Claim count: 44 — arithmetic: dossier §9 register has 109 rows (clm-ca-001…109); 39 taken verbatim plus 5 adapted/trimmed (002, 026, 027, 053, 097) = 44. Excluded: 6 assessed unverified (018, 019, 033, 038, 050, 089) — excluded from the article by rule; 59 dossier-only rows. The count is 9 over the ~35 aim because the event spans five debated questions (offering, Gen 4:7, mark, sevenfold, bloodguilt) plus 12 connections, and Yonatan's Decisions 1 and 3 added the mark-clarification claim (080) and the Hittite re-grounding claim (053); Phase 2 carried four dossier-only rows into the register (002, 003, 052, 070) so every prose statement has a corresponding in-register claim. Word counts are the validator's countWords method, which includes the three Ancient World subsection headings (Ancient World 400 by that method, 386 prose-only). Adaptations: clm-ca-002 trimmed to the established manuscript date and provenance (the scribal-curriculum and composition-date parts are not asserted); clm-ca-026 trimmed to the mummy and its tattoos (the Ramesside date and body locations are not asserted in the claim; the prose keeps 'Ramesside mummy'); clm-ca-027 reworded with 'probably' added; clm-ca-053 assessment simplified to 'Probable.' (the HL §6 caveat and the established generalisation are not asserted); clm-ca-097 trimmed to the established MT speech ellipsis (the LXX/Samaritan supply 'Let us go into the field' is unverified and is NOT part of the claim). Each adapted claim's evidence records its trim; clm-ca-001's evidence marks its four print-edition citations as not read in full text. Yonatan's editorial decisions (2026-11-14, overriding the drafting brief's conservative choices): (1) the mark's racial interpretations stay in the dossier, but the article carries exactly one brief sentence (Ancient World, mark subsection): Scripture does not identify the mark's appearance or connect it with skin color; no history of the misreading is recounted in the article; clm-ca-080 (racist misreading, established false) is included, clm-ca-081 (LDS restriction/disavowal) stays dossier-only, and the LDS essay (S11, verified institutional page) is not cited in the article; (2) Luke 11:51 is RETAINED as conn-ca-012, a supporting parallel to the primary conn-ca-011 (Matthew 23:35) — both retained, Matthew primary; (3) every article claim and quotation rests ONLY on dossier §12.1 verified-from-full-text sources: the abbuttum claim (030) was dropped because Hammurabi §§226–227/146 were consulted only via search-result text, not opened in full, and the abbuttum sentence was cut from the prose; the kin-choice sentence was re-grounded on the opened Encyclopedia.com synthesis via clm-ca-053 (Hittite Laws/Telipinu, probable) and clm-ca-040 (Barmash thesis via the opened Bloch article, probable) — the Mari letters (041) stay dossier-only; the Nuzi parallel (second-hand via Westermann) and Wenham's word-count statistic (second-hand via Christ Over All) do not enter the article; no second-hand position is presented as verified anywhere in this draft — second-hand attributions inside claim evidence (Stade, Cassuto, Gevirtz, Williams, Liedke, Turretin, Duhm et al., the HALOT/DCH citations inside Christ Over All) are labelled as such there; the inaccessible scholarship (Wenham 1987, Hamilton 1990, Sarna 1989, Cassuto 1961, von Rad 1972, Brueggemann 1982, Speiser 1964, Kugel 1997, Byron 2011, Mellinkoff 1981) was attempted (archive.org controlled lending; Google Books API HTTP 429 — blocked, do not repeat; Scribd/JSTOR paywalls) and NO position is attributed to any of those authors in this draft; Mettinger 2007 / Walton 2015 / HALOT / DCH were not consulted and no exception has been granted for this event (the A&E exception does not extend) — none of the §9 claims rests on them. Disagreements preserved as debated, not resolved: the seven header disagreements (mark on the body or not; material explanation; heart reading; Gen 4:6–7 corrupt vs later addition; Nuzi parallel; Wenham's statistic; qayin etymology) — the Nuzi parallel, Wenham's statistic, and the qayin-as-smith reading (083) are dossier-only. Convention notes applied: 'debated — verdict: no' is a verdict on the claim as phrased, not a §8 confidence label; 'unverified' is a verification status, not a confidence label; 'established false' and 'established absence' are verdicts on the claim as phrased.
